[FrontMatterHeading] Abstract
[Normal] Training a robot with reinforcement learning requires a delicate integration of a physics simulator, be it headless, a python environment, a reward function, a learning algorithm, monitoring and policy evaluation. Although existing frameworks provide these capabilities, setting them up normally requires simulator-specific pre-existing knowledge and programming experience. EasyRTG, my application, addresses this barrier through a no-code desktop workflow in which a user imports a robot in Universal Robot Description Format (URDF) and describes the required behaviour, reviews an assistant-generated environmental configuration and reward function, validates the reward, trains a policy and evaluates the result.
[Normal] My system combines a Flutter desktop interface, a Fast API orchestration backend, PyBullet inspection of the imported robot and reward testing, and NVIDIA Isaac Sim training and playback. EasyRTG derives control-relevant robot structure directly from the URDF and represents rewards as well-crafted mathematical expressions. This removes fixed joint-name rules and predefined reward items, allowing my application pipeline to support quadruped and humanoid robots.
[Normal] EasyRTG was run in 40+ simulation runs with few on the Unitree A1 robot, the ANYmal robot. The rest of the runs were on the Unitree Go1 robot, and the NASA Valkyrie robot both employing PPO, SAC and TD3. Of the 40 runs, 34 led to policies that were deemed useful. 12 out of those 34 analyzable cases, reached at least 95% of the 1000-step episode limit, with peak performance reaching around 32,000 environment steps per second on a single RTX 5000 GPU.
[Normal] Best policies of PPO, SAC, and TD3 reached completion rates of 96.3%, 100%, and 99.1% respectively on the Go1, PPO, and SAC. The Valkyrie painted a different picture though, SAC was at 82.1%, PPO and TD3 around 20%. The selection of an algorithm is a much more significant factor.
[Normal] The evaluation also shows that a high reward does not necessarily represent the intended robot behaviour. On the galloping task of GO1 robot, TD3 algorithm produced a fast trot without a true flight phase required for galloping. EasyRTG demonstrates a working integration of language-assisted configuration along with general robot inspection and accelerated learning.

[Heading1] 1  Introduction
[Heading2] 1.1 Project motivation
[Normal] Reinforcement learning is closed loop in which an agent observes the state of an environment its put into, selects an action form the available options, and receives a reward based on the selected action [1]. Applying this closed loop to robot control requires considerale work and understanding of tools and techniques. The user should first set up a simulator and read the robot model, then load the robot and create the observations and actions, design the reward function, set the training parameters, execute the training process, and judge the performance of policy after training.
[Normal] Existing RL libraries simplify the method of usage as much as possible, but they usually assume that the user already has the knowledge to build a valid environment [2]. This requirement introduces a challenge for new users, a dependency of knowledge of each tool on each part of the workflow. Designing the reward is impossible without understanding and interpreting the state is impossible without understanding the robot and the simulator.
[Normal] EasyRTG project motivated by a previous robotics project where the robot could learn the desired behavior, but by the time it truly learnt, a significant amount of manual work and time that had been done in integrating the simulator, the environment code, the reward function, the training scripts and the visualization. This underlying effort wasn't reflected in the final demonstration. EasyRTG was thus born, making environment creation and experiment management a product of the application and not an undocumented prerequisite.
[Normal]

[Heading2] 1.2 Problem statement
[Normal] Currently, many different, unrelated skills must be implemented to convert a raw robot description and a specified task into a working reinforcement learning environment. Today's physics engines and RL toolkits can do it, but they're essentially low-level scripted and configured, and they rely on convention that varies based on the simulator. A standard URDF file specifies physical geometry and the hierarchy of the joints, but it does not specify the most important learning parameters: which degrees of freedom to actuate, allowed contact links, reset distributions, reward formulation.  The robot's physical structure and the desired movement needs to be manually translated into environmental code which ensures reliable training. In this project, it is explored if this translation can be achieved by an integrated and inspectable desktop GUI, without resorting to low-level simulator programming, while maintaining the control of the user.
[Heading2] 1.3 Aim and objectives
[Normal] The aim of this project was to develop a desktop platform that takes a user from a URDF robot and a natural-language objective to a trained and evaluated policy without requiring simulator or reinforcement-learning code. The objectives were to:
[ListBullet] Provide a single desktop workflow for robot inspection, configuration, monitoring, training and evaluation.
[ListBullet] Derive the morphology required for control directly from the URDF without relying on robot-specific joint-name rules.
[ListBullet] Allow an LLM assistant to propose reward expressions and configuration changes while keeping consequential actions reviewable and subject to user approval.
[ListBullet] Use GPU-parallel simulation to make repeated robot-learning experiments practical on a single workstation.
[ListBullet] Evaluate the platform across multiple robot bodies, tasks and learning algorithms using saved telemetry and recorded behaviour.
[Heading2] 1.4 Research questions
[Normal] The implementation and evaluation were guided by the following four research questions.

[Heading2] 1.5 Scope and contributions
[Normal] EasyRTG is a single user desktop robot simulator application for URDF robots. These contributions include an integrated workflow, name-based configuration system, expression-based rewards feature, manual configuration auditing, controlled ai assistant and retained run provenance. No new reinforcement-learning algorithm is proposed in the project.
[Normal] The scope of my project does not include any physical deployment of the robot, terrain curricula, camera observation, ROS integration and multi-agent learning. Therefore, the evaluation only shows evidence of a platform that can configure and train multiple simulated legged robots. It does not give evidence of the transfer to the physical hardware or access to multiple users simultaneously.

[Normal] Chapter 2 provides an overview of the reinforcement-learning and GPU-native simulation algorithms, reward-design research and related accessibility platforms used in this work. In the 3rd chapter, the design-science methodology, sources of evidence, requirements and experimental protocol are described. The system architecture and the main technical mechanisms are presented in Chapter 4. The iterative development process has been explained in Chapter 5. The experiments and results of my simulation runs are shown in Chapter 6. The research questions are answered along with the limitations of study in Chapter 7. The conclusion and future work is presented in chapter 8.
[Heading1] 2  Background and Literature Survey
[Heading2] 2.1 Reinforcement learning for robot control
[Normal] In reinforcement learning, a policy selects actions from observations and is improved using rewards collected through interaction with an environment [1]. This formulation is suitable for robotics because the desired behaviour can be specified without providing a labelled action for every possible state. However, continuous action spaces, contact dynamics and long training horizons increase both learning instability and the cost of reward-design errors [2]. Robot policies are therefore normally trained in simulation before they are considered for physical deployment. All experiments in this report were conducted in simulation.
[Heading2] 2.2 The three learners: PPO, SAC and TD3
[Normal] Three algorithms were selected for the evaluation. Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) is an on-policy method that limits destructive policy updates through a clipped surrogate objective [3]. Its simplicity and reliable implementations have made it a common baseline for locomotion. Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) is an off-policy method that maximises expected return together with policy entropy [4], thereby maintaining exploration in continuous-control tasks. Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (TD3) addresses value overestimation through twin critics, delayed policy updates and target-policy smoothing [5].
[Normal] EasyRTG initially supported PPO only. SAC and TD3 were added after the pipeline had demonstrated that a robot could learn, allowing the evaluation to examine whether different learners produced different outcomes under the same task configuration.

[Heading2] 2.3 From single environments to massively parallel simulation
[Normal] Gym standardised the interface between an agent and an environment [6], while Gymnasium and Stable-Baselines3 provided maintained APIs and implementations on which the first EasyRTG CPU training lane was built [7, 8]. PyBullet provided a lightweight method for loading URDF models, inspecting joints and validating state calculations [9]. These tools were suitable for checking individual robot instances, but could not provide the volume of experience required by the final locomotion experiments. This limitation motivated the GPU training architecture described in Chapter 4.
[Heading2] 2.4 Isaac Gym and the GPU-native turn
[Normal] Makoviychuk et al. demonstrated that physics simulation and policy learning can remain on the GPU, removing the CPU transfer bottleneck and increasing throughput by orders of magnitude [10]. For EasyRTG, this approach enabled thousands of robot environments to run in parallel rather than one environment at a few hundred steps per second. The resulting throughput made repeated locomotion experiments feasible on a single workstation; the measured performance is reported in Section 6.4.
[Heading2] 2.5 Orbit and Isaac Lab
[Normal] Mittal et al. introduced Orbit, a modular framework for robot-learning environments based on Isaac Sim that was later developed into Isaac Lab [11]. Orbit demonstrates the structure that a well-designed environment framework can provide, but its Python environment definitions are intended for developers. EasyRTG uses Isaac Lab as its training substrate [12] while placing its configuration behind the desktop workflow. The underlying capability is retained without requiring the user to author an Isaac Lab environment directly.
[Heading2] 2.6 Learning to walk in minutes
[Normal] Rudin et al. trained thousands of simulated ANYmal robots to walk within minutes on a single GPU [13]. Their result established an important performance reference and motivated the initial use of ANYmal in this project. However, the reported speed relied on an environment, reward and curriculum designed specifically for that robot. EasyRTG required ten ANYmal attempts before one run reached 95% of the episode limit (Appendix D). This difference illustrates the current cost of supporting a general no-code workflow rather than a specialist robot implementation.
[Heading2] 2.7 Reward design as the real bottleneck
[Normal] A reward is an optimisation target rather than a neutral description of a task. An agent may therefore exploit any difference between the intended behaviour and the quantity that is measured. Potential-based shaping preserves an optimal policy under specific conditions [14], but practical locomotion rewards combine objectives and penalties for which this guarantee does not generally hold. Henderson et al. and Engstrom et al. further show that implementation details and evaluation choices can materially affect deep-reinforcement-learning results [15, 16].
[Normal] This literature supports treating reward authoring as a correctness problem, not only as a configuration task. EasyRTG therefore compiles and audits reward expressions before GPU training begins. The evaluation also reports episode length and behavioural measures alongside reward. Section 6.7 provides a direct example of the underlying risk: a policy achieved a high galloping reward without performing a true gallop.
[Heading2] 2.8 Eureka: language models writing rewards
[Normal] Ma et al. demonstrated through Eureka that a large language model can generate reward code and refine it using training feedback, achieving human-competitive reward design across several tasks [17]. Eureka is the closest published precedent for the EasyRTG assistant, but the two systems make different safety trade-offs. Eureka generates executable reward code and searches over it evolutionarily. EasyRTG generates expressions over an approved state vocabulary; these expressions are compiled through an AST whitelist and audited on synthetic state ranges before they can be saved. EasyRTG therefore accepts less expressive freedom in exchange for inspectability and controlled tool use.
[Heading2] 2.9 DrEureka: pushing language-assisted design toward hardware
[Normal] DrEureka extended language-assisted reward design towards sim-to-real transfer by using a language model to generate both reward and domain-randomisation configurations [18]. This work also identifies an important boundary of EasyRTG. The present system stops at a recorded policy in simulation and does not implement domain randomisation or hardware deployment. These capabilities are therefore included in the future-work requirements in Section 8.2.
[Heading2] 2.10 General-purpose simulators: Gazebo and Unity ML-Agents
[Normal] Gazebo provides a general robot simulator with programmatic interfaces and extensive ROS integration [19], while Unity ML-Agents turns game-engine scenes into learning environments [20]. Gazebo offers broad robotics support but requires substantial setup. Unity ML-Agents provides flexible visual environments but requires engine-specific authoring. Both platforms are more capable than EasyRTG within their intended domains; however, the path from a robot model to a trained policy still requires code and framework-specific knowledge.
[Heading2] 2.11 Unity RL Playground: the closest accessibility claim
[Normal] The Unity RL Playground presented by Ye et al. is the closest published system to the accessibility objective of EasyRTG, providing one-click locomotion training for imported mobile robots [21]. EasyRTG differs by exposing a shared state vocabulary for reward authoring, performing a reward audit before training, and retaining a run archive for later examination. The published description of Unity RL Playground does not report reward authoring at the same level of detail, although its stated scope is narrower.
[Heading2] 2.12 Where EasyRTG sits
[Normal] The literature provides established learning algorithms, high-throughput simulators and methods for language-assisted reward generation. The remaining accessibility problem is their integration into a coherent workflow. EasyRTG addresses this gap by making robot structure, reward semantics, training controls and supporting evidence visible within one application. Its contribution is therefore the design and evaluation of this integration, including an account of where the abstraction succeeds and where expert judgement remains necessary.

[Heading1] 3  Research Methodology and Requirements
[Heading2] 3.1 Design-science approach
[Normal] A design-science approach was adopted because the research questions concern both the design of an integrated tool and its behaviour when applied [22]. Knowledge was developed by building and evaluating the EasyRTG artefact rather than through observation alone. The process was iterative: a barrier was identified, a mechanism was implemented, its behaviour was evaluated, and the design was refined. This process follows the stages proposed by Peffers et al.: problem identification, definition of objectives, design and development, demonstration, evaluation and communication [23]. Chapter 5 records how these stages were repeated during development.
[Heading2] 3.2 Evidence sources
[Normal] The evaluation used four evidence sources. First, 50 Git commits between 11 June and 14 August 2026 record the sequence of architectural changes. Second, the source code and automated tests establish which functions were implemented. Third, each Isaac run retains its configuration and telemetry, allowing the numerical results in Chapter 6 to be recomputed from the archive. Finally, recorded policy videos provide behavioural evidence that cannot be obtained from reward and episode statistics alone.
[Normal] One inclusion rule was applied throughout the analysis: timestamped directories containing numeric reward telemetry were included as analysable runs, while directories without telemetry were retained as pre-telemetry failures. This rule explains why the run count in this report is higher than the count presented in the earlier project presentation.

[Heading2] 3.4 Experimental protocol and metrics
[Normal] The run archive contains experiments conducted between 13 July and 18 August 2026 on a single RTX 5000. The analysable set contains 34 runs: eight A1 PPO, ten ANYmal PPO, four Go1 PPO, three Go1 SAC, two Go1 TD3, three Valkyrie PPO, three Valkyrie SAC and one Valkyrie TD3. This distribution is unbalanced. The comparisons in Chapter 6 are therefore reported as observed project results rather than as a statistically complete benchmark.
[Normal] The primary measures were mean episode reward, mean episode length and environment steps per second. Task-specific measures included forward velocity, uprightness, lateral drift and flight phase. Episode length is reported as a fraction of the 1,000-step limit because it indicates whether the robot remained stable for the episode. Fleet summaries select the run with the highest observed reward for each robot-algorithm pairing. This improves readability but introduces best-run selection bias, which is addressed in Section 7.3.
[Heading2] 3.5 Software verification
[Normal] Software verification was performed by running the backend test suite in a new temporary directory with third-party pytest plugin autoloading disabled. The result was 256 passing tests, one skipped test and no failures. The tests cover configuration phases, expression compilation, morphology, contact state, episode timing, Isaac bridge calculations, action authoring, spawn height and smoke behaviour. The Flutter command-line tool did not return in the available environment; consequently, no current claim is made about frontend analysis or test status. This limitation is recorded in Section 7.3.
[Heading1] 4  System Design and Architecture
[Heading2] 4.1 Architectural overview
[Normal] The architecture must support thousands of parallel GPU environments while keeping the desktop responsive. EasyRTG separates the user interface from local orchestration to satisfy both requirements. Flutter provides the desktop interface [24]. FastAPI manages application state, exposes REST and streaming endpoints, supervises workers and records project state [25]. The LLM assistant has no privileged access and calls the same bounded tools used by the application. Simulation is divided into a lightweight inspection lane and a GPU training lane, preventing simple checks from consuming a training session.
[Normal] 
[Caption] Figure 2. EasyRTG architecture, and the separation between the inspection and GPU training lanes.
[Normal] The principal mechanisms follow the order of the workflow: the robot structure is inspected, a reward is defined against that structure, and the assistant then supports configuration and execution. This ordering ensures that assistant proposals are grounded in the inspected robot and the available state vocabulary.
[Heading2] 4.2 URDF inspection and morphology
[Normal] The first prototype inferred robot roles from link and joint names such as 'hip', 'foot' and 'ankle'. This approach failed when naming conventions changed. The resulting morphology layer instead treats the URDF as a kinematic tree. It identifies the base link, movable joints, leaf structures, candidate limbs and contact links from connectivity and joint properties. Standing height and spawn height are measured relative to the robot rather than copied from a sample model. Dimensionless signals such as height_ratio and upright can therefore retain the same meaning for quadruped and humanoid robots.
[Normal] Morphology inference does not make every URDF automatically trainable. Poor inertial values, unrealistic joint limits and ambiguous contact geometry may still require calibration. Its contribution is narrower: a new robot is configured from structural evidence rather than from naming rules written for a previous model.
[Heading2] 4.3 Expression rewards and the shared state vocabulary
[Normal] After the robot structure has been derived, the required behaviour must be expressed as a reward. An early fixed catalogue allowed users to select only predefined components. Although simple, this approach restricted the range of behaviours and required application changes for every new task. EasyRTG instead represents each reward term as a mathematical expression over a shared state vocabulary, including forward_velocity, upright, height_ratio, mean(contact), flight_phase and episode_progress. Vector widths are supplied by the morphology layer, so mean(contact) has the same interpretation whether the robot has two, four or six contact limbs.
[Normal] Safety is provided through compilation rather than a restricted catalogue. Expressions are parsed into an abstract syntax tree and accepted only when every node is whitelisted. Attribute access and subscripting are excluded, preventing arbitrary Python execution. Configuration patches compile every enabled expression before saving. A separate audit evaluates reward scale over synthetic state ranges and flags non-finite values, dominant penalties, all-penalty designs and sums that depend on the number of degrees of freedom. These checks cannot guarantee successful learning, but they detect several expensive failure classes before a GPU run begins.
[Heading2] 4.4 Assistant and human oversight
[Normal] The assistant makes expression-based configuration accessible to users who would not write the expressions directly. It can inspect robot details, calibrate a goal, patch a configuration, test a reward, start or stop training and inspect previous runs. Basic requests can be routed to a local Ollama model, while more complex goal interpretation can use an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The system prompt provides the robot-specific vocabulary and available reward priors.
[Normal] Tools that change configuration or control runs remain subject to explicit user approval. This design follows human-AI interaction guidance that recommends communicating system capabilities, making changes visible and preserving correction or undo [26]. The approval step introduces friction, but ensures that consequential actions remain reviewable and recoverable.
[Normal] 
[Caption] Figure 3. The EasyRTG desktop assistant, showing a generated training configuration and the changes offered for review.
[Heading2] 4.5 Training, monitoring and evaluation
[Normal] After a configuration is approved, Isaac training runs in a separate subprocess under Isaac Sim's Python environment and follows the installed Isaac Lab workflow [12]. The worker writes telemetry to a file, which the backend follows and streams to the Flutter charts. Every run retains its environment configuration, observation and action contracts, checkpoints, log and evaluation video. Live evaluation can launch NVIDIA's WebRTC client, while recorded evaluation runs headlessly and produces an MP4 file that can be replayed inside the desktop application.
[Normal] Retained evidence is required because a reward curve cannot show whether a humanoid is walking forward, drifting sideways or merely remaining upright. The interpretation of several experiments in Chapter 6 depends on the saved configuration, term-level telemetry and recorded video. Run provenance is therefore part of the evaluation mechanism rather than only a storage feature.
[Heading1] 5  Implementation and Iterative Development
[Heading2] 5.1 From proposal to working system
[Normal] The original proposal described a six-week, CPU-first application based on PyBullet, Gymnasium and PPO from Stable-Baselines3. It was intended to run on an average laptop and to use predefined reward components with optional custom Python. The completed system differs from this plan in each area that introduced significant technical risk. Training moved to NVIDIA Isaac Sim on a GPU, custom Python rewards were removed, predefined reward components became audited expressions, and joint-name rules were replaced by morphology inference. The evaluation also expanded from PPO on sample robots to three algorithms across four robot families.
[Normal] These changes do not indicate that the proposal failed. Instead, the prototype exposed requirements that could not have been established from the initial design alone. The following development history identifies the failures and observations that produced each major revision.

[Heading2] 6.3 What the reward actually paid for
[Normal] Because reward totals are not comparable across robots, the more informative question is which terms produced a policy's score. EasyRTG logs every reward term separately, allowing the total to be decomposed at the point of highest observed performance.
[Normal] 
[Caption] Figure 6. Term-by-term decomposition of the reward at the peak-reward step of the best Go1 run.
[Normal] Three positive terms dominate the decomposition: forward velocity at 1.49, staying alive at 0.50 and uprightness at 0.49. The penalties are between one and four orders of magnitude smaller. Effort is the largest penalty at -0.060, while joint-limit violation is effectively zero at -0.00017, indicating that the policy was not operating against its joint limits.
[Normal] Interpretation. The decomposition confirms that the policy earned its score primarily by moving forward while upright. It also shows that the penalties provided little constraint. A reward dominated by positive terms remains vulnerable to the type of misspecification demonstrated in Section 6.7, supporting the audit mechanism described in Section 4.3.
[Heading2] 6.4 Throughput and the GPU lane
[Normal] 
[Caption] Figure 7. Peak simulation throughput against the number of parallel environments, coloured by robot.
[Normal] The highest measured throughput was 32,056.8 environment steps per second, achieved by A1 at 4,096 environments. Go1 also exceeded 30,000 steps per second in recorded runs, while Valkyrie remained below approximately 14,600 steps per second at every tested batch size.
[Normal] Increasing the number of environments provides more parallel work, but robot morphology determines the cost of each simulated step. A humanoid with more joints and bodies is therefore not directly comparable with a quadruped. RQ4 is explained by the interaction of two factors: parallelism determines the available workload, while robot complexity sets the practical throughput ceiling. The two diagnostic runs at 16 environments both remained below 100 steps per second, approximately three hundred times slower than the same robots at 4,096 environments.
[Heading2] 6.5 How long learning took
[Normal] Experiment cost depends on both simulation throughput and the number of steps required for learning. Learning time was measured as the number of environment steps before the smoothed mean episode length first remained above 900. This threshold indicates sustained stability rather than a single favourable logging interval.
[Normal] Exactly twelve runs crossed this threshold, matching the twelve runs that reached 95% of the episode limit through a separately calculated measure. Appendix C provides the complete ordering. The best ANYmal run crossed after 2.51M steps, while the slowest successful Go1 run required 17.60M steps. Faster stabilisation did not imply a higher final reward. The highest-reward A1 run (20260728-202311; reward 4,767.0) required 16.42M steps to stabilise, whereas an earlier A1 run stabilised after 4.03M steps and achieved less than half that reward. Learning speed and final score must therefore be reported separately.

[Normal] Go1 was the only robot evaluated with all three learners at the same environment count, making it the most suitable three-algorithm comparison.

[Heading2] 6.7 Go1 walking and galloping
[Normal] The Go1 experiments demonstrate how reward semantics define learned behaviour. The walking reward encouraged forward motion, uprightness and sustained ground contact. The galloping reward additionally required a flight phase in which all four feet left the ground. In the presentation experiments, the walking policy travelled at 0.98 m/s, achieved an uprightness of 0.99 and survived 963 steps. The galloping policy reached 1.38 m/s, survived the full episode and was airborne for 43% of the stride. The robot and training budget were unchanged; only the reward semantics differed.
[Normal] 
[Caption] Figure 9. The Unitree Go1 during recorded policy evaluation.
[Normal] The three-algorithm comparison exposed a limitation in the galloping reward. TD3 achieved the highest velocity, approximately 1.65 m/s, but had the lowest flight fraction at 29%. SAC was slower at 1.52 m/s but achieved a 52% flight fraction. TD3 had therefore learned a fast trot that scored well without producing the intended gallop.
[Normal] Interpretation. This outcome is the reward-misspecification failure predicted by the literature [14, 15]. It demonstrates why contact-state measurements and video inspection must accompany reward. A high reward alone is insufficient evidence that the intended task has been learned.

[Heading2] 6.9 Functional verification
[Normal] The 256 passing backend tests provide a second form of evidence. They do not demonstrate learned robot behaviour. Instead, they verify the mechanisms required to interpret the training results: morphology handling, action mapping, state vocabulary, expression guards, episode clocks, contact signals, Isaac bridge calculations, configuration phases, and failure handling.
[Normal] Neither form of evidence is sufficient in isolation. A visually convincing gait does not guarantee configuration safety, and passing standard checks offers no way to determine whether the output produces useful locomotion or something fundamentally unstable. The galloping result from Section 6.7 demonstrates this clearly, it satisfied every software check yet produced an unintended gait pattern rather than a functional motion. This gap between automated verification and behavioural evaluation confirms that both are required at once.
[Heading1] 7  Discussion
[Heading2] 7.1 Answering the research questions
[Normal] RQ1: configuration with human oversight. EasyRTG breaks configuration into structural checks, relative calibration, and reward writing against an approved vocabulary. Compiling and auditing occur automatically before any tool runs. Users do not edit the underlying environment source code at all. A comparative user study measuring time savings has not yet been conducted.
[Normal] RQ2: applicability across robot bodies. Treating morphology and state terms as dimensionless values allows one pipeline to generate viable policies for the A1, ANYmal, and Go1 quadrupeds alongside the Valkyrie humanoid. This approach removes fixed geometric constraints that typically constrain standard simulation pipelines. The test results confirm it functions correctly across these specific URDF models. It cannot however support manipulators or wheeled robots without significant architectural changes.
[Normal] RQ3: differences between learners. All three algorithms produced nearly identical performance caps when controlling the Go1 quadruped. PPO, SAC, and TD3 showed negligible variance in final reward values within that specific environment. The Valkyrie results tell a different story entirely. SAC became the only viable option for that platform while neither PPO nor TD3 achieved stable gait patterns. Uneven algorithm coverage and incomplete hyperparameter tuning weaken these conclusions.
[Normal] RQ4: simulation throughput. Parallel environments allowed throughput to scale until robot physics created a hard ceiling. A single GPU processed 32,056 steps per second across 4,096 environments for the A1 configuration. Valkyrie performed below that threshold due to increased rigid-body solver latency from its mass and joint count. These figures align with the architectural shifts toward Isaac detailed in Section 5.2, which matches GPU simulation benchmarks published by Castano [10] and Garcia [13].
[Heading2] 7.2 What the project learned about abstraction
[Normal] The core design challenge involved determining exactly which layers of complexity must remain visible. Obscuring simulator installation failed to eliminate underlying hardware constraints or operating system dependencies; the MJX experiment demonstrated this when sandboxed execution could not isolate itself from host GPU drivers. Arbitrary Python allows unconstrained state mutations that compromise the runtime, while a static reward catalogue avoids these security risks but remains insufficient for environments requiring complex logic. EasyRTG resolved this by exposing only the inputs that drive learning, observations, actions, and termination signals, while compiling the rest of the execution logic into a controlled backend.
[Normal] Defining the precise scope of the assistant proved significantly more difficult. The system generates configuration files that must pass validation before execution, functioning strictly as a drafting tool within a framework of human oversight. Project findings rely on concrete metrics, specifically six pre-telemetry failures alongside dozens of short-lived policies. Language models simplify the initial setup phase but cannot replace expert diagnosis; investigation into the Valkyrie TD3 failure confirmed that automated tools miss critical physics errors, ultimately requiring manual inspection of the URDF file.
[Heading2] 7.3 Limitations and threats to validity
[ListBullet] The testing matrix favors certain configurations over others.
[ListBullet] SAC and TD3 targeted the Go1 and Valkyrie platforms while A1 and ANYmal were limited to PPO alone, preventing any broad claims about cross-robot algorithm consistency.
[ListBullet] Fleet summaries highlight the single most successful run per pairing rather than tracking an average across random seeds.
[ListBullet] These metrics reflect peak observed capability rather than expected typical performance.
[ListBullet] Throughput tests relied on one RTX 5000, so those numbers cannot be treated as universal benchmarks for other hardware.
[ListBullet] Every policy was evaluated strictly in simulation, omitting domain randomization or physical transfer.
[ListBullet] The no-code argument stands as an architectural benefit at this stage rather than a verified fact; without user studies measuring task completion or errors, empirical validation remains unestablished.
[ListBullet] Training outcomes remain dependent on the URDF file itself because automatic inference cannot fix bad mass distribution or incorrect joint limits hidden inside it.
[ListBullet] Observations remained locked at seven keys despite flexible rewards; camera feeds, terrain mapping, ROS networking, and multi-agent support remain unimplemented.
[ListBullet] Final verification focused strictly on backend logic because the Flutter tool failed to run properly in the test environment, leaving frontend status completely unconfirmed.
[Heading2] 7.4 Practical and academic significance
[Normal] The practical contribution of EasyRTG is an integrated path from a robot file to a recorded policy, combining configuration, training and supporting evidence within one application. Its academic contribution is a case study of language-assisted reward design without unrestricted code execution. The heterogeneous run archive also demonstrates why reward, episode survival and task-specific behaviour must be evaluated together.
[Normal] The project does not demonstrate that robot learning has become effortless. Its more defensible contribution is that important configuration decisions are made visible, reviewable and repeatable. When a decision is incorrect, as in the galloping reward, the retained evidence makes the error identifiable.
[Heading1] 8  Conclusion and Future Work
[Heading2] 8.1 Conclusion
[Normal] This work establishes an integrated desktop platform enabling users to import a URDF robot, define a locomotion task in natural language, and train reinforcement learning policies without writing low-level simulator scripts. All five primary objectives outlined in Chapter 1 were satisfied.
[Normal] The system relies on a Flutter frontend, a FastAPI-orchestrated backend, PyBullet-based parameter inspection, and training within the NVIDIA Isaac Sim simulator using GPU hardware to autonomously extract motion physics directly from the URDF tree. Rewards are captured and audited as evaluated mathematical expressions via an established vocabulary facilitated by an LLM operating under strictly confined user validation protocols. The complete application underwent analysis across thirty-four Isaac Sim runs utilising four distinct robot families and three continuous-control algorithms.
[Normal] Three significant outcomes defined the experimental trials. Parallel execution on the GPU eliminated the CPU bottleneck for multi-platform learning, achieving a peak throughput of 32,056.8 environment steps per second at a single workstation level using an RTX 5000 GPU. For quadruped models such as the Go1, learner selection exerted minimally significant influence over final outcomes; PPO, SAC, and TD3 achieved greater than ninety-six percent survival episodes and converged upon comparable reward scores. Conversely, algorithm choice directly dictated training viability on higher-dimensional platforms like the Valkyrie humanoid. SAC emerged as the solitary method maintaining stable balance throughout its simulation, reaching an eighty-two point one percent survival score while PPO and TD3 plateaued at twenty percent, with TD3 subsequently degrading into numerical instability.
[Normal] The engineering process was fundamentally driven by mitigating failures encountered during iterative integration. Initial challenges necessitated the inclusion of robot-relative floor-falling terminations, while fragile rule-based naming conventions were discarded in favour of a robust kinematic tree traversal mechanism. Directories and safety concerns regarding arbitrary Python execution mandated an AST expression compiler, whereas galloping traversal conditions informed the explicit modelling of foot surface contact states within Isaac Sim.
[Normal] A notable limitation arose during the Go1 galloping test, where imprecise reward specifications drove TD3 to emulate a rapid trot movement. This unintended locomotion mode accumulated exceptionally high scalar rewards, causing the platform to entirely omit required airtime during its motion phase. The experiment confirms that unconstrained total reward volumes serve insufficiently as indicators of actual movement behaviour; without monitoring contact signals, episode length, and preliminary videos, unregulated reward accumulation remains practically insignificant. Finally, while the internal AI assistant frequently achieved functional reward functions from natural language inputs, it nonetheless requires a significantly expanded validation set to guarantee robustness in complex engineering scenarios.
[Normal] The application evolved from its initial CPU-based conceptualisation into a fully operational pipeline. This progression demonstrates that robotic locomotion, reward design, and GPU-assisted training can be consolidated into a single no-code desktop platform while maintaining strict user oversight.
[Heading2] 8.2 Future work
[Normal] The first priority is a controlled usability study. A comparison between the EasyRTG workflow and a documented code-based baseline should measure task completion time, configuration errors, requests for assistance and a validated usability scale. This study is required to evaluate the no-code claim empirically rather than infer it from the architecture.
[Normal] Observation expressions and per-episode velocity commands should also be introduced together, allowing one policy to respond to changing instructions rather than a fixed goal. A campaign worker could then propose, audit and test reward revisions automatically while retaining the user-approval mechanism described in Section 4.4.
[Normal] Further work should add terrain and sensor observations, improve automatic dynamics checks, evaluate more robots with balanced seeds and algorithm budgets, and measure throughput on additional GPUs. Hyperparameters should be studied through a reproducible optimisation framework such as Optuna [27] rather than through individual experiments alone. Finally, domain randomisation and hardware export are required before EasyRTG can claim a complete route from simulation to physical robot behaviour. DrEureka provides a relevant model for this stage [18].

[FrontMatterHeading] Abstract
[Normal] Training a robot with reinforcement learning requires a delicate integration of a physics simulator, be it headless, a python environment, a reward function, a learning algorithm, monitoring and policy evaluation. Although existing frameworks provide these capabilities, setting them up normally requires simulator-specific pre-existing knowledge and programming experience. EasyRTG, my application, addresses this barrier through a no-code desktop workflow in which a user imports a robot in Universal Robot Description Format (URDF) and describes the required behaviour, reviews an assistant-generated environmental configuration and reward function, validates the reward, trains a policy and evaluates the result.
[Normal] My system combines a Flutter desktop interface, a Fast API orchestration backend, PyBullet inspection of the imported robot and reward testing, and NVIDIA Isaac Sim training and playback. EasyRTG derives control-relevant robot structure directly from the URDF and represents rewards as well-crafted mathematical expressions. This removes fixed joint-name rules and predefined reward items, allowing my application pipeline to support quadruped and humanoid robots.
[Normal] EasyRTG was run in 40+ simulation runs with few on the Unitree A1 robot, the ANYmal robot. The rest of the runs were on the Unitree Go1 robot, and the NASA Valkyrie robot both employing PPO, SAC and TD3. Of the 40 runs, 34 led to policies that were deemed useful. 12 out of those 34 analyzable cases, reached at least 95% of the 1000-step episode limit, with peak performance reaching around 32,000 environment steps per second on a single RTX 5000 GPU.
[Normal] Best policies of PPO, SAC, and TD3 reached completion rates of 96.3%, 100%, and 99.1% respectively on the Go1, PPO, and SAC. The Valkyrie painted a different picture though, SAC was at 82.1%, PPO and TD3 around 20%. The selection of an algorithm is a much more significant factor.
[Normal] The evaluation also shows that a high reward does not necessarily represent the intended robot behaviour. On the galloping task of GO1 robot, TD3 algorithm produced a fast trot without a true flight phase required for galloping. EasyRTG demonstrates a working integration of language-assisted configuration along with general robot inspection and accelerated learning.

[Heading1] 1  Introduction
[Heading2] 1.1 Project motivation
[Normal] Reinforcement learning is closed loop in which an agent observes the state of an environment its put into, selects an action form the available options, and receives a reward based on the selected action [1]. Applying this closed loop to robot control requires considerale work and understanding of tools and techniques. The user should first set up a simulator and read the robot model, then load the robot and create the observations and actions, design the reward function, set the training parameters, execute the training process, and judge the performance of policy after training.
[Normal] Existing RL libraries simplify the method of usage as much as possible, but they usually assume that the user already has the knowledge to build a valid environment [2]. This requirement introduces a challenge for new users, a dependency of knowledge of each tool on each part of the workflow. Designing the reward is impossible without understanding and interpreting the state is impossible without understanding the robot and the simulator.
[Normal] EasyRTG project motivated by a previous robotics project where the robot could learn the desired behavior, but by the time it truly learnt, a significant amount of manual work and time that had been done in integrating the simulator, the environment code, the reward function, the training scripts and the visualization. This underlying effort wasn't reflected in the final demonstration. EasyRTG was thus born, making environment creation and experiment management a product of the application and not an undocumented prerequisite.
[Normal]

[Heading2] 1.2 Problem statement
[Normal] Currently, many different, unrelated skills must be implemented to convert a raw robot description and a specified task into a working reinforcement learning environment. Today's physics engines and RL toolkits can do it, but they're essentially low-level scripted and configured, and they rely on convention that varies based on the simulator. A standard URDF file specifies physical geometry and the hierarchy of the joints, but it does not specify the most important learning parameters: which degrees of freedom to actuate, allowed contact links, reset distributions, reward formulation.  The robot's physical structure and the desired movement needs to be manually translated into environmental code which ensures reliable training. In this project, it is explored if this translation can be achieved by an integrated and inspectable desktop GUI, without resorting to low-level simulator programming, while maintaining the control of the user.
[Heading2] 1.3 Aim and objectives
[Normal] The aim of this project was to develop a desktop platform that takes a user from a URDF robot and a natural-language objective to a trained and evaluated policy without requiring simulator or reinforcement-learning code. The objectives were to:
[ListBullet] Provide a single desktop workflow for robot inspection, configuration, monitoring, training and evaluation.
[ListBullet] Derive the morphology required for control directly from the URDF without relying on robot-specific joint-name rules.
[ListBullet] Allow an LLM assistant to propose reward expressions and configuration changes while keeping consequential actions reviewable and subject to user approval.
[ListBullet] Use GPU-parallel simulation to make repeated robot-learning experiments practical on a single workstation.
[ListBullet] Evaluate the platform across multiple robot bodies, tasks and learning algorithms using saved telemetry and recorded behaviour.

[Heading1] 2  Background and Literature Survey
[Heading2] 2.1 Reinforcement learning for robot control
[Normal] In reinforcement learning, a policy selects actions from observations and is improved using rewards collected through interaction with an environment [1]. This formulation is suitable for robotics because the desired behaviour can be specified without providing a labelled action for every possible state. However, continuous action spaces, contact dynamics and long training horizons increase both learning instability and the cost of reward-design errors [2]. Robot policies are therefore normally trained in simulation before they are considered for physical deployment. All experiments in this report were conducted in simulation.
[Heading2] 2.2 The three learners: PPO, SAC and TD3
[Normal] Three algorithms were selected for the evaluation. Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) is an on-policy method that limits destructive policy updates through a clipped surrogate objective [3]. Its simplicity and reliable implementations have made it a common baseline for locomotion. Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) is an off-policy method that maximises expected return together with policy entropy [4], thereby maintaining exploration in continuous-control tasks. Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (TD3) addresses value overestimation through twin critics, delayed policy updates and target-policy smoothing [5].
[Normal] EasyRTG initially supported PPO only. SAC and TD3 were added after the pipeline had demonstrated that a robot could learn, allowing the evaluation to examine whether different learners produced different outcomes under the same task configuration.

[Heading2] 2.3 From single environments to massively parallel simulation
[Normal] Gym standardised the interface between an agent and an environment [6], while Gymnasium and Stable-Baselines3 provided maintained APIs and implementations on which the first EasyRTG CPU training lane was built [7, 8]. PyBullet provided a lightweight method for loading URDF models, inspecting joints and validating state calculations [9]. These tools were suitable for checking individual robot instances, but could not provide the volume of experience required by the final locomotion experiments. This limitation motivated the GPU training architecture described in Chapter 4.
[Heading2] 2.4 Isaac Gym and the GPU-native turn
[Normal] Makoviychuk et al. demonstrated that physics simulation and policy learning can remain on the GPU, removing the CPU transfer bottleneck and increasing throughput by orders of magnitude [10]. For EasyRTG, this approach enabled thousands of robot environments to run in parallel rather than one environment at a few hundred steps per second. The resulting throughput made repeated locomotion experiments feasible on a single workstation; the measured performance is reported in Section 6.4.
[Heading2] 2.5 Orbit and Isaac Lab
[Normal] Mittal et al. introduced Orbit, a modular framework for robot-learning environments based on Isaac Sim that was later developed into Isaac Lab [11]. Orbit demonstrates the structure that a well-designed environment framework can provide, but its Python environment definitions are intended for developers. EasyRTG uses Isaac Lab as its training substrate [12] while placing its configuration behind the desktop workflow. The underlying capability is retained without requiring the user to author an Isaac Lab environment directly.
[Heading2] 2.6 Learning to walk in minutes
[Normal] Rudin et al. trained thousands of simulated ANYmal robots to walk within minutes on a single GPU [13]. Their result established an important performance reference and motivated the initial use of ANYmal in this project. However, the reported speed relied on an environment, reward and curriculum designed specifically for that robot. EasyRTG required ten ANYmal attempts before one run reached 95% of the episode limit (Appendix D). This difference illustrates the current cost of supporting a general no-code workflow rather than a specialist robot implementation.
[Heading2] 2.7 Reward design as the real bottleneck
[Normal] A reward is an optimisation target rather than a neutral description of a task. An agent may therefore exploit any difference between the intended behaviour and the quantity that is measured. Potential-based shaping preserves an optimal policy under specific conditions [14], but practical locomotion rewards combine objectives and penalties for which this guarantee does not generally hold. Henderson et al. and Engstrom et al. further show that implementation details and evaluation choices can materially affect deep-reinforcement-learning results [15, 16].
[Normal] This literature supports treating reward authoring as a correctness problem, not only as a configuration task. EasyRTG therefore compiles and audits reward expressions before GPU training begins. The evaluation also reports episode length and behavioural measures alongside reward. Section 6.7 provides a direct example of the underlying risk: a policy achieved a high galloping reward without performing a true gallop.
[Heading2] 2.8 Eureka: language models writing rewards
[Normal] Ma et al. demonstrated through Eureka that a large language model can generate reward code and refine it using training feedback, achieving human-competitive reward design across several tasks [17]. Eureka is the closest published precedent for the EasyRTG assistant, but the two systems make different safety trade-offs. Eureka generates executable reward code and searches over it evolutionarily. EasyRTG generates expressions over an approved state vocabulary; these expressions are compiled through an AST whitelist and audited on synthetic state ranges before they can be saved. EasyRTG therefore accepts less expressive freedom in exchange for inspectability and controlled tool use.
[Heading2] 2.9 DrEureka: pushing language-assisted design toward hardware
[Normal] DrEureka extended language-assisted reward design towards sim-to-real transfer by using a language model to generate both reward and domain-randomisation configurations [18]. This work also identifies an important boundary of EasyRTG. The present system stops at a recorded policy in simulation and does not implement domain randomisation or hardware deployment. These capabilities are therefore included in the future-work requirements in Section 8.2.
[Heading2] 2.10 General-purpose simulators: Gazebo and Unity ML-Agents
[Normal] Gazebo provides a general robot simulator with programmatic interfaces and extensive ROS integration [19], while Unity ML-Agents turns game-engine scenes into learning environments [20]. Gazebo offers broad robotics support but requires substantial setup. Unity ML-Agents provides flexible visual environments but requires engine-specific authoring. Both platforms are more capable than EasyRTG within their intended domains; however, the path from a robot model to a trained policy still requires code and framework-specific knowledge.
[Heading2] 2.11 Unity RL Playground: the closest accessibility claim
[Normal] EasyRTG's goal of accessibility is closest to the Unity RL Playground presented by Ye et al. which gives one-click locomotion training to mobile robots imported into the Unity platform [21]. EasyRTG is different in that it provides a common vocabulary of states for writing the rewards, it conducts a reward audit prior to training, and it maintains a history of runs for analysis. The published description of Unity RL Playground is available and does not detail reward authoring as much as its scope is more limited.
[Heading2] 2.12 Where EasyRTG sits
[Normal] The literature provides established learning algorithms, high-throughput simulators and methods for language-assisted reward generation. The remaining accessibility problem is their integration into a coherent workflow. EasyRTG addresses this gap by making robot structure, reward semantics, training controls and supporting evidence visible within one application. Its contribution is therefore the design and evaluation of this integration, including an account of where the abstraction succeeds and where expert judgement remains necessary.

[Heading1] 3  Research Methodology and Requirements
[Heading2] 3.1 Design-science approach
[Normal] A design-science approach was adopted because the research questions concern both the design of an integrated tool and its behaviour when applied [22]. Knowledge was developed by building and evaluating the EasyRTG artefact rather than through observation alone. The process was iterative: a barrier was identified, a mechanism was implemented, its behaviour was evaluated, and the design was refined. This process follows the stages proposed by Peffers et al.: problem identification, definition of objectives, design and development, demonstration, evaluation and communication [23]. Chapter 5 records how these stages were repeated during development.
[Heading2] 3.2 Evidence sources
[Normal] The evaluation used four evidence sources. First, 50 Git commits between 11 June and 14 August 2026 record the sequence of architectural changes. Second, the source code and automated tests establish which functions were implemented. Third, each Isaac run retains its configuration and telemetry, allowing the numerical results in Chapter 6 to be recomputed from the archive. Finally, recorded policy videos provide behavioural evidence that cannot be obtained from reward and episode statistics alone.

[Normal] The run archive contains experiments conducted between 13 July and 18 August 2026 on a single RTX 5000. The analysable set contains 34 runs: eight A1 PPO, ten ANYmal PPO, four Go1 PPO, three Go1 SAC, two Go1 TD3, three Valkyrie PPO, three Valkyrie SAC and one Valkyrie TD3. This distribution is unbalanced. The comparisons in Chapter 6 are therefore reported as observed project results rather than as a statistically complete benchmark.
[Normal] The primary measures were mean episode reward, mean episode length and environment steps per second. Task-specific measures included forward velocity, uprightness, lateral drift and flight phase. [Heading1] 4  System Design and Architecture
[Heading2] 4.1 Architectural overview
[Normal] The architecture must support thousands of parallel GPU environments while keeping the desktop responsive. EasyRTG separates the user interface from local orchestration to satisfy both requirements. Flutter provides the desktop interface [24]. FastAPI manages application state, exposes REST and streaming endpoints, supervises workers and records project state [25]. The LLM assistant has no privileged access and calls the same bounded tools used by the application. Simulation is divided into a lightweight inspection lane and a GPU training lane, preventing simple checks from consuming a training session.
[Normal] 
[Caption] Figure 2. EasyRTG architecture, and the separation between the inspection and GPU training lanes.
[Normal] The principal mechanisms follow the order of the workflow: the robot structure is inspected, a reward is defined against that structure, and the assistant then supports configuration and execution. This ordering ensures that assistant proposals are grounded in the inspected robot and the available state vocabulary.
[Heading2] 4.2 URDF inspection and morphology
[Normal] The first prototype inferred robot roles from link and joint names such as 'hip', 'foot' and 'ankle'. This approach failed when naming conventions changed. The resulting morphology layer instead treats the URDF as a kinematic tree. It identifies the base link, movable joints, leaf structures, candidate limbs and contact links from connectivity and joint properties. Standing height and spawn height are measured relative to the robot rather than copied from a sample model. Dimensionless signals such as height_ratio and upright can therefore retain the same meaning for quadruped and humanoid robots.
[Normal] Morphology inference does not make every URDF automatically trainable. Poor inertial values, unrealistic joint limits and ambiguous contact geometry may still require calibration. Its contribution is narrower: a new robot is configured from structural evidence rather than from naming rules written for a previous model.
[Heading2] 4.3 Expression rewards and the shared state vocabulary
[Normal] After the robot structure has been derived, the required behaviour must be expressed as a reward. An early fixed catalogue allowed users to select only predefined components. Although simple, this approach restricted the range of behaviours and required application changes for every new task. EasyRTG instead represents each reward term as a mathematical expression over a shared state vocabulary, including forward_velocity, upright, height_ratio, mean(contact), flight_phase and episode_progress. Vector widths are supplied by the morphology layer, so mean(contact) has the same interpretation whether the robot has two, four or six contact limbs.
[Normal] Safety is provided through compilation rather than a restricted catalogue. Expressions are parsed into an abstract syntax tree and accepted only when every node is whitelisted. Attribute access and subscripting are excluded, preventing arbitrary Python execution. Configuration patches compile every enabled expression before saving. A separate audit evaluates reward scale over synthetic state ranges and flags non-finite values, dominant penalties, all-penalty designs and sums that depend on the number of degrees of freedom. These checks cannot guarantee successful learning, but they detect several expensive failure classes before a GPU run begins.
[Heading2] 4.4 Assistant and human oversight
[Normal] The assistant makes expression typed configuration accessible to the user that would not write the expressions directly. It can look up robot information, set a goal, adjust a configuration, run a test of a reward, and start or stop training, as well as look at previous runs. Simple requests can be directed to a local Ollama model, and complex goal interpretation can be done via an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The available reward priors and robot specific vocabulary is given by the system prompt.
[Normal] Tools that change configuration or control runs continue to be subject to explicit approval from the user. This design has been inspired by human-AI interaction guidance to communicate the capabilities of the system, to make changes visible and to keep the possibility of correction or undo [26]. The approval process adds friction, and makes sure that actions that follow are reviewable and reversible.
[Normal]

[Heading2] 4.5 Training, monitoring and evaluation
[Normal] Once a configuration has been approved Isaac training runs in a separate subprocess within the Isaac Sim Python environment and proceeds with the same flow as the installed Isaac Lab workflow [12]. The worker writes telemetry to a file, then the backend follows it on the file and streams it to theflutter charts. Environment configuration, observation and action contracts, checkpoints, log and evaluation video are all saved for each run. Live evaluation starts NVIDIA's WebRTC client and recorded evaluation is executed headless and generates an MP4 file which can be replayed in the desktop application.
[Normal] Evidence must be retained because without it, a reward curve cannot indicate if a humanoid is walking forward, drifting sideways or simply standing upright. The interpretation of several experiments in Chapter 6 relies on the use of the saved configuration, telemetry at the term level and recorded video. So run provenance is a feature of the evaluation mechanism as well as a feature for storage.

[Heading2] 5.1 From proposal to working system
[Normal] The original idea was to use a six-week, CPU-first application using PyBullet, Gymnasium and PPO in Stable Baselines3. In each area where there was an element of significant technical risk, the completed system differs from this plan. Training was switched to NVIDIA Isaac Sim on a GPU, the custom Python rewards were replaced with and become audited expressions, and the joint-name rules were replaced with morphology inference. The evaluation was also expanded to three algorithms for four robot families, instead of PPO on sample robots.

[Heading2] 6.1 Run coverage and failure history
[Normal] The earlier project presentation summarised 30 runs up to 3 August 2026, while the README later reported 32. A final scan for this report identified 40 timestamped run directories.
