[Heading2] 6.3 What the reward actually paid for
[Normal] Because reward totals are not comparable across robots, the more informative question is which terms produced a policy's score. EasyRTG logs every reward term separately, allowing the total to be decomposed at the point of highest observed performance.
[Normal] 
[Caption] Figure 6. Term-by-term decomposition of the reward at the peak-reward step of the best Go1 run.
[Normal] Three positive terms dominate the decomposition: forward velocity at 1.49, staying alive at 0.50 and uprightness at 0.49. The penalties are between one and four orders of magnitude smaller. Effort is the largest penalty at -0.060, while joint-limit violation is effectively zero at -0.00017, indicating that the policy was not operating against its joint limits.
[Normal] Interpretation. The decomposition confirms that the policy earned its score primarily by moving forward while upright. It also shows that the penalties provided little constraint. A reward dominated by positive terms remains vulnerable to the type of misspecification demonstrated in Section 6.7, supporting the audit mechanism described in Section 4.3.
[Heading2] 6.4 Throughput and the GPU lane
[Normal] 
[Caption] Figure 7. Peak simulation throughput against the number of parallel environments, coloured by robot.
[Normal] The highest measured throughput was 32,056.8 environment steps per second, achieved by A1 at 4,096 environments. Go1 also exceeded 30,000 steps per second in recorded runs, while Valkyrie remained below approximately 14,600 steps per second at every tested batch size.
[Normal] Increasing the number of environments provides more parallel work, but robot morphology determines the cost of each simulated step. A humanoid with more joints and bodies is therefore not directly comparable with a quadruped. RQ4 is explained by the interaction of two factors: parallelism determines the available workload, while robot complexity sets the practical throughput ceiling. The two diagnostic runs at 16 environments both remained below 100 steps per second, approximately three hundred times slower than the same robots at 4,096 environments.
[Heading2] 6.5 How long learning took
[Normal] The amount of simulation throughput and the number of steps needed to learn affects experiment cost. The number of environment steps before the first time the smoothed mean episode length exceeded 900 was used as a metric for learning time. This threshold represents a 'stable interval' and not a single favourable logging interval.
[Normal] This number of runs has been exceeded exactly 12 times (twelve runs in the same measure with a separate calculation which is equal to 95% of the limit for the episode). A full ordering is given in Appendix C. The best ANYmal run was achieved after 2.51M steps and the slowest successful run with Go1 was after 17.60M steps. This did not mean that the reward was greater if the stabilisation was completed more quickly. The most rewarding A1 run (20260728-202311; reward 4,767.0) took 16.42M steps to stabilise, while a previous A1 run took less than half that number of steps and had a reward of only 2,102.5. The learning speed and score at the end of the learning need to be reported separately, therefore.
[Heading2] 6.6 Go1: three learners, one solved robot
[Normal] Go1 was the only robot evaluated with all three learners at the same environment count, making it the most suitable three-algorithm comparison.
[Normal] 
[Caption] Figure 8. Reward for the best Go1 run under each learner, at 4,096 environments with the same reward expression.
[Normal] All three Go1 policies converged to within 8% on reward: SAC reached 2,250.1, TD3 reached 2,112.7 and PPO reached 2,073.9. Episode survival was also similar at 100%, 99.1% and 96.3% of the limit respectively. The traces differ mainly in shape. SAC improves in distinct stages, PPO improves more smoothly, and TD3 rises fastest initially before flattening.
[Normal] Interpretation. These results do not establish that the algorithms are equivalent. They show that the Go1 task was sufficiently tractable for all three learners to approach saturation. The comparison provides a baseline in which the pipeline does not visibly favour one learner. The more difficult Valkyrie task in Section 6.8 provides the separating case.
[Heading2] 6.7 Go1 walking and galloping
[Normal] The Go1 experiments demonstrate how reward semantics define learned behaviour. The walking reward encouraged forward motion, uprightness and sustained ground contact. The galloping reward additionally required a flight phase in which all four feet left the ground. In the presentation experiments, the walking policy travelled at 0.98 m/s, achieved an uprightness of 0.99 and survived 963 steps. The galloping policy reached 1.38 m/s, survived the full episode and was airborne for 43% of the stride. The robot and training budget were unchanged; only the reward semantics differed.
[Normal] 
[Caption] Figure 9. The Unitree Go1 during recorded policy evaluation.
[Normal] A three-algorithm comparison revealed one caveat of the galloping reward. TD3 had the highest velocity, ~1.65 m/s, and lowest flight fraction, 29%. SAC was slower at 1.52 m/s and was able to reach a flight fraction of 52%. TD3 had consequently developed a quick trot that gained good marks without the desired gallop.
[Normal] Interpretation. This is the result of the failure to specify rewards as predicted by the literature [14, 15]. It helps to illustrate the need to use contact-state measurement and video inspection in combination with reward. A high reward does not mean the task to be performed is learned.
[Heading2] 6.8 Valkyrie: a controlled algorithm comparison
[Normal] The strongest controlled comparison in the archive is between SAC and TD3 on Valkyrie. Both runs use the same reward expression and a 40M-step budget, holding the tested configuration constant except for the learner.
[Normal] 
[Caption] Figure 10. Reward for Valkyrie under SAC and TD3, same reward expression and same 40M-step budget.
[Normal] 
[Caption] Figure 11. Episode length reveals that SAC's advantage came from staying upright, not from scoring faster.
[Normal] For around 20 million steps, there was no significant difference between both learners in both methods. They are then diverged in their behaviour. SAC achieved its highest average reward at 1283.8 and the average episode length was 821.0 steps. TD3 stayed around 200 steps of survival, got to 287.0 of best reward, and then stalled afterwards, producing NaN observations. The dotted line in the figures is the failure line.
[Normal] The policies were compared at their best checkpoints, for which they received broadly similar reward per step. SAC got a bigger total because it added these up for about four times as many steps before it dropped out. So it wasn't a more points-per-minute advantage, it was about saving the episode. Before failure, TD3 also revealed several orders of magnitude growth in reward terms, which suggest a critic or numerical failure and not just a failure to take a step forward.
[Normal] 
[Caption] Figure 12. The NASA Valkyrie during recorded SAC policy evaluation.
[Normal] Interpretation. Learner choice materially affected the Valkyrie outcome under the tested configuration, with SAC producing substantially longer survival than TD3. This is a result for one task and configuration, not evidence that SAC is generally superior. The limits of the comparison are discussed in Section 7.3.
[Heading2] 6.9 Functional verification
[Normal] The other evidence is from the 256 passing backend unit tests. Not exhibiting learned robot behaviours. Rather, they check the mechanisms that need to be interpreted in order to translate the results of the training: handling of morphology, mapping of actions, vocabulary of the states, action guards, episode timers, contact signals, calculations of the Isaac bridge, configuration phases, and failure handling.
[Normal] Both types of evidence are needed alone to be sufficient. Visual realism of gait does not imply gait-safety, and standard gait checks will not reveal if the gait produced by the output is an effective gait or whether it is fundamentally unsafe. This is evident in the galloping result from Section 6.7 which passed all the software tests, but generated an unintended gait pattern instead of a functional gait. This difference between automated verification and behavioural evaluation is a testament to the need for both at the same time.
[Heading1] 7  Discussion
[Heading2] 7.1 Answering the research questions
[Heading2] RQ1: With human supervision configuration. EasyRTG splits configuration up into: structural checks, relative calibration and writing rewards on a ratified word stock. Compiling and auditing is performed automatically, prior to any tool running. The user does not modify in any way the source code of the underlying environment. A comparative user study, measurement of time savings, has not yet been conducted.
[Heading2] RQ2: applicability with respect to robot bodies. By using the terms of morphology and state as dimensionless values, one pipeline can be used to create policies for the A1 quadruped, the ANYmal quadruped, the Go1 quadruped and the Valkyrie humanoid. This method does away with the rigid geometric restrictions that are typically associated with conventional simulation pipelines. The test results indicate that it works in these particular URDF models. However, without major architectural changes it cannot be used to support manipulators or wheeled robots.
[Heading2] RQ3: Differences between Learners. Almost identical performance limits were achieved by all three algorithms in the control of the Go1 quadruped. PPO, SAC and TD3 had very little deviation in the final values of the rewards in that environment. It's a different story when it comes to the Valkyrie results. SAC was the sole stable gait pattern achieved on that platform with PPO and TD3 not producing stable gait patterns. Conclusions are hindered by the lack of even distribution of algorithms and by inadequate hyperparameter tuning.
[Heading2] RQ4: simulation throughput. Throughput was increased up until a hard ceiling arose from robot physics – using parallel environments. For the A1 configuration, a single GPU processed 32,056 steps per second, in 4,096 environments. Valkyrie was below that because of the higher number of masses and joints that it has. The numbers correspond to the architectural changes with respect to Isaac presented in Section 5.2, and are similar to the GPU simulation benchmarks provided by Castano [10] and Garcia [13].
[Heading2] 7.2 What the project learned about abstraction
[Normal] The biggest design problem was what layers of complexity needed to be exposed. But hiding simulator installation did not remove hardware limitations or OS dependency as with the MJX experiment which could not separate itself from the host GPU drivers through sandboxed execution. Arbitrary Python enables unrestricted state changes which make the runtime unsafe, while a static reward catalogue is safe, but too simple to handle environments where more advanced logic is required. EasyRTG solved this by only exposing those inputs that are used to stimulate learning, observations, actions and termination signals, and the remainder of the logic to be executed by the agent was compiled into a controlled backend.
[Normal] It was much harder to define exactly what the assistant could do. The system produces configuration files which are then validated prior to being executed and thus remain a drafting tool under human control. Project results are based on hard data, such as six failures before the telemetry and a number of short-term policies. Although language models can help with the initial setup process, they don't provide expert diagnosis: investigation into the Valkyrie TD3 failure revealed that automated tools missed key physics mistakes, and the final conclusion was to manually check the URDF file.
[Heading2] 7.3 Limitations and threats to validity
[ListBullet] The testing matrix favors certain configurations over others.
[ListBullet] SAC and TD3 targeted the Go1 and Valkyrie platforms while A1 and ANYmal were limited to PPO alone, preventing any broad claims about cross-robot algorithm consistency.
[ListBullet] Fleet summaries highlight the single most successful run per pairing rather than tracking an average across random seeds.
[ListBullet] These metrics reflect peak observed capability rather than expected typical performance.
[ListBullet] Throughput tests relied on one RTX 5000, so those numbers cannot be treated as universal benchmarks for other hardware.
[ListBullet] Every policy was evaluated strictly in simulation, omitting domain randomization or physical transfer.
[ListBullet] The no-code argument stands as an architectural benefit at this stage rather than a verified fact; without user studies measuring task completion or errors, empirical validation remains unestablished.
[ListBullet] Training outcomes remain dependent on the URDF file itself because automatic inference cannot fix bad mass distribution or incorrect joint limits hidden inside it.
[ListBullet] Observations remained locked at seven keys despite flexible rewards; camera feeds, terrain mapping, ROS networking, and multi-agent support remain unimplemented.
[ListBullet] Final verification focused strictly on backend logic because the Flutter tool failed to run properly in the test environment, leaving frontend status completely unconfirmed.
[Heading2] 7.4 Practical and academic significance
[Normal] EasyRTG's bottom-line is a step from a robot file to a recorded policy, one application for configuration, training and supporting evidence. It is a case study of design of an unstrict code-executing reward system that is based on language, academically. The heterogeneous run archive also shows the importance of separately and task-specifically evaluating reward and episode survival and behaviour.
[Normal] The project does not reflect the simplicity of robot learning. An important contribution it makes is that important configuration decisions are made visible, reviewable and repeatable. Evidence is kept and is evident of the wrong decision (for example the galloping reward).
[Heading1] 8  Conclusion and Future Work
[Heading2] 8.1 Conclusion
[Heading2] This work brings together an integrated desktop platform for taking in one URDF robot file and outputting one locomotion task in natural language, and for training RL policies directly without having to write low level simulator scripts. Each of the five main goals listed in Chapter 1 were met.
[Heading2] It involves autonomously extracting motion physics from the URDF tree, using NVIDIA Isaac Sim simulator on GPU hardware for training, PyBullet for parameter inspection and a Flutter frontend, and a FastAPI-orchestrated backend. Rewards are expressed using a limited set of vocabulary (assessed math expressions are validated) and an LLM (under user validation process). All the application was analysed using the Isaac Sim running 34 times with four different families of robots and three different continuous control algorithms.
[Heading2] There were three significant outcomes of the experimental trials. In the case of multi-platform learning, the CPU was eliminated as the learning process' bottleneck, and parallel execution on the GPU was used, where the maximum throughput at the single workstation level with the RTX 5000 GPU was 32,056.8 environment steps per second. The impact of learner selection was at best weakly significant for quadrupedal models such as the Go1 and all three models (PPO, SAC, TD3) achieved a high number of survival episodes with over ninety six percent and converged to similar reward scores. Conversely, algorithm choice was a direct contributor to the training viability of more dimensional platforms, like the Valkyrie humanoid. Among the three methods, only SAC maintained the stable balance throughout the entire simulation and resulted in an eighty two point one percent survival rate, whereas PPO and TD3 had a maximum of twenty percent survival rates but then became numerically unstable at later stages.
[Heading2] The iterative integration was mediated by means of failure, as the engineering process was motivated primarily in this way. At first, it was necessary to introduce the robot relative floor falling terminations and to give up fragile rule based naming, in favour of a more powerful traversal mechanism of kinematic tree. The galloping traversal conditions led to the need for explicit foot surface contact states modelling in Isaac Sim; Directories and safety issues around arbitrary Python execution necessitated the need for an AST expression compiler.
[Heading2] One note was that TD3 was not sufficiently "rewarded" with the Go1 galloping test and so it was emulating a fast trot gait. This also received an unwanted locomotion mode, and the platform failed to reach required height of airtime during the locomotion phase, which was also given very high scalar reward. As demonstrated in this experiment, unconstrained total reward volumes are not sufficient on their own to indicate the actual movement behaviour – if it is not monitored using contact signals and episode length and seen from the preliminary videos, it is of little consequence. Lastly, although the internal AI assistant was able to sometimes successfully produce functional reward functions from natural language input, it still needs a much larger validation set to ensure it is robust in complex engineering situations.
[Heading2] The application started as a CPU-based conceptual application, and was developed into an actual pipeline. This route indicates that, this can be combined with a single no code desktop platform, under strict supervision of the users, by incorporating the parts of the robots locomotion, reward design and training by using a GPU.
[Heading2] 8.2 Future work
[Normal] A controlled usability test is the number one priority. When using the EasyRTG workflow, the time to complete the task, number of configuration errors, and the need for assistance and a validated usability scale should be compared to a baseline documented code. This no-code claim would need to be verified in the course of this study, and it does not appear this can be taken for granted from the architecture.
[Normal] Also, a policy should only be sensitive to changes in instructions – not a fixed goal – otherwise, observe and velocity commands should be introduced at the same time within a single episode. Then a campaign worker could propose and run tests/ audits of changes to the rewards (but would still have to have a user-approval process as described in 4.4.).
[Normal] Other items to consider for future research include including terrain and sensor observations, enhancing automatic dynamics checks, testing additional robots with similar seeds and algorithm budgets, and quantifying the throughput on other GPUs. Instead of just exploring by individual experiments, hyperparameters should be explored from a reproducible optimisation perspective, e.g., Optuna [27]. Lastly, it is required to have domain randomisation (and hardware export) before EasyRTG can boast of having a complete simulation to real robot behaviour path. This stage is provided with a model relevant to DrEureka [18].
